MULTI-MEMBER LLC OPERATING AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme Ventures, LLC

FORMATION AND MEMBERSHIP
Acme Ventures, LLC is a limited liability company organized under the laws of Delaware, owned by more than one member as set forth below.

MEMBERS, CONTRIBUTIONS, AND OWNERSHIP
Acme Ventures, LLC has the following members, initial capital contributions, and ownership interests:

Member: _______________________ Contribution: $_______________ Ownership: _______%
Member: _______________________ Contribution: $_______________ Ownership: _______%
Member: _______________________ Contribution: $_______________ Ownership: _______%
(Add additional lines as needed. Ownership percentages should total 100%.)

FEDERAL TAX CLASSIFICATION
For federal tax purposes, Acme Ventures, LLC is, by default, classified as a partnership — its income, deductions, and credits pass through to its members' own tax returns, rather than Acme Ventures, LLC paying tax at the entity level, unless Acme Ventures, LLC affirmatively elects a different classification.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "unless the entity elects otherwise, a domestic eligible entity is— (i) A partnership if it has two or more members; or (ii) Disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, default federal tax classification of eligible entities (the 'check-the-box' rule) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  Known gap: This default applies automatically, with no election required — but it isn't the only option. A multi-member LLC can elect to be taxed as a corporation, or potentially as an S corporation through a separate election, by filing the appropriate IRS form. This document doesn't say which classification is actually better for a given business — that depends on income level, self-employment tax exposure, and other facts specific to the business. Partnership tax treatment brings its own requirements this document doesn't cover, including that the LLC generally must file its own annual information return (Form 1065) even though it doesn't pay entity-level tax itself. This is one federal regulation; no additional independent source was found restating this specific default classification separately.

HOW AND WHEN A DIFFERENT CLASSIFICATION GETS ELECTED
Changing away from the default disregarded-entity treatment isn't automatic — it takes filing IRS Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election). The effective date on that form has real limits: it can't be dated more than 75 days before the filing date, and can't be dated more than 12 months after it. Once Acme Ventures, LLC makes an election to change its classification, it generally can't elect a different classification again for 60 months from the effective date of that election, absent IRS permission.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "an eligible entity may elect to be classified other than as provided under paragraph (b) of this section, or to change its classification, by filing Form 8832, Entity Classification Election, with the service center designated on Form 8832."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(i) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, how an eligible entity elects its classification (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  "The effective date specified on Form 8832 can not be more than 75 days prior to the date on which the election is filed and can not be more than 12 months after the date on which the election is filed."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, the effective-date window for a classification election (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  "If an eligible entity makes an election under paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section to change its classification (other than an election made by an existing entity to change its classification as of the effective date of this section), the entity cannot change its classification by election again during the sixty months succeeding the effective date of the election."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iv) (Cornell LII text), Treasury Regulations, the sixty-month limitation on re-electing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.7701-3)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current Treasury Regulations text. The 60-month lock-in has a narrow exception — the IRS may allow an earlier change if more than half the entity's ownership as of the later election is held by people who owned no interest at the time of the earlier one — but that relief isn't automatic, and this document doesn't state the full standard for obtaining it. This document doesn't cover the separate, S-corporation-specific election under 26 U.S.C. § 1362, which has its own timing rule.

LIMITED LIABILITY
Acme Ventures, LLC's debts and liabilities are its own — they don't become a member's personal debts or liabilities solely because that person is a member.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability shield (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  "A member of a limited liability company shall be subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and shall also be personally liable under a judgment of a court or for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company, whether that liability or obligation arises in contract, tort, or otherwise, under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for any debt, obligation, or liability of the corporation; except that the failure to hold meetings of members or managers or the failure to observe formalities pertaining to the calling or conduct of meetings shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that a member or the members have alter ego or personal liability for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company where the articles of organization or operating agreement do not expressly require the holding of meetings of members or managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, alter ego liability and the meeting-formalities carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used here as real evidence that a liability shield with a specific, real exception is a genuine feature of LLC law generally — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company. The shield isn't absolute: a member can still be held personally liable under the common-law 'alter ego' doctrine, the same doctrine that can pierce a corporation's liability shield, under the same or similar circumstances. One thing that specifically does not count against a member on its own, at least under this statute: failing to hold formal member or manager meetings doesn't establish alter ego liability by itself, as long as the articles of organization or the operating agreement itself doesn't require holding them.

RECORDS AND TAX RETURN ACCESS
A member — or someone a member's interest in Acme Ventures, LLC has been transferred to — has the right, for purposes reasonably related to their interest, to inspect and copy Acme Ventures, LLC's required records during normal business hours, and to obtain a written copy of Acme Ventures, LLC's federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year, promptly after they become available.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Each member, manager, and transferee has the right, upon reasonable request, for purposes reasonably related to the interest of that person as a member, manager, or transferee, to each of the following: (1) To inspect and copy during normal business hours any of the records required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (2) To obtain in writing from the limited liability company, promptly after becoming available, a copy of the limited liability company’s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, member and transferee inspection and tax-return rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.10.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This right belongs to a transferee (someone who receives an economic interest, such as an heir, without becoming a full member) as well as to members themselves — it isn't limited to people with voting rights. This document doesn't restate the additional annual and interim financial-reporting duties this same statute imposes once an LLC has more than 35 members.

MANAGEMENT AND VOTING
Acme Ventures, LLC is: ☐ Member-managed  ☐ Manager-managed

If manager-managed, the manager(s): _______________________________________________

Ordinary business decisions require the vote or written consent of members holding more than 50% of the ownership interests, unless this agreement requires a greater vote for a specific decision. Admitting a new member, amending this agreement, and selling substantially all of the company's assets each require the unanimous vote or written consent of all members.

FIDUCIARY DUTIES — AND WHO ACTUALLY OWES THEM
Which management box is checked above changes who owes what to whom. If Acme Ventures, LLC is member-managed, each member owes the company and the other members a duty of loyalty — to account for and hold as trustee any property, profit, or benefit the member takes from the company or a company opportunity; to avoid dealing with the company on behalf of someone whose interests are adverse to it; and to avoid competing with the company — plus a duty of care limited to avoiding grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law (ordinary negligence isn't enough to breach it). If Acme Ventures, LLC is manager-managed instead, those same duties shift to the manager or managers — a member who isn't also a manager owes no fiduciary duty to the company or the other members solely because they're a member.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "A member’s duty of loyalty to the limited liability company and the other members is limited to the following: (1) To account to the limited liability company and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the member in the conduct and winding up of the activities of a limited liability company or derived from a use by the member of a limited liability company property, including the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity. (2) To refrain from dealing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company as or on behalf of a person having an interest adverse to the limited liability company. (3) To refrain from competing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member's duties of loyalty and care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  "In a manager-managed limited liability company, all of the following rules apply: (1) Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members. (2) Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers. (3) Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.09.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default duty structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. A member doesn't breach these duties merely by acting in their own self-interest — the statute says so directly. Everyone still owes the company and the other members an obligation of good faith and fair dealing, regardless of which management structure applies; that obligation isn't one of the two duties that shifts to managers only.

DISTRIBUTIONS
Distributions of available cash or property are made among the members as set forth in this agreement. Members may set any distribution arrangement they choose in this document — it doesn't have to match ownership percentages.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Any distributions made by a limited liability company before its dissolution and winding up shall be among the members in accordance with the operating agreement. If the operating agreement does not otherwise provide, distributions shall be on the basis of the value, as stated in the required records when the limited liability company decides to make the distribution, of the contributions the limited liability company has received from each member"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.04(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default distribution rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.04.)
  "Unless the articles of organization or written operating agreement provides otherwise, a person’s dissociation does not entitle the person to a distribution"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.04(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation doesn't itself trigger a distribution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17704.04.)
  Known gap: This is one state's default rule, useful as real evidence of what happens if an operating agreement doesn't actually state how distributions are shared: rather than splitting by ownership percentage, the default is based on the value of each member's contributions. That default can produce a genuinely surprising result — a member with a stated ownership percentage that doesn't match their actual capital contribution (a common setup for a member contributing services rather than cash) could receive far less than their ownership percentage would suggest, or nothing at all, unless the agreement itself sets a different rule. Separately, under this same default framework, a member who leaves the company isn't automatically entitled to a distribution just because they left, unless the company's governing documents say otherwise. This is exactly why this document states the members' agreed-upon arrangement directly, rather than leaving it to whatever the state default happens to be. This is one state's default rule, cited as real evidence — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company.

THE DEFAULT DISSOLUTION TRIGGERS
Absent a different rule in the operating agreement or articles of organization, state law dissolves an LLC on the first of several events: an event the operating agreement or articles specifically designate; a vote of members holding 50% or more of the voting interests (or a higher percentage, if the operating agreement sets one); 90 consecutive days with no members at all; or a court's decree of judicial dissolution.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "A limited liability company is dissolved, and its activities shall be wound up, upon the happening of the first to occur of the following: (a) On the happening of an event set forth in a written operating agreement or the articles of organization. (b) By the vote of 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the members of the limited liability company or a greater percentage of the voting interests of members as may be specified in the articles of organization, or a written operating agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default dissolution triggers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.01.)
  "The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the limited liability company has no members, except that, on the death of a natural person who is the sole member of a limited liability company, the status of the member, including a membership interest, may pass to one or more heirs, successors, and assigns of the member by will or applicable law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the no-members trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.01.)
  "Entry of a decree of judicial dissolution pursuant to Section 17707.03."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the judicial-dissolution trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.01.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default trigger set — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The statutory member-vote default is 50% or more, not a majority exceeding 50% — a small but real difference from a "more than half" threshold, worth checking against whatever specific vote requirement this agreement's own management section actually sets. This document doesn't cover the separate grounds for judicial dissolution itself, which is a distinct statutory process from the events listed here.

DISSOLUTION
Acme Ventures, LLC will continue until dissolved by the vote or written consent of members holding more than 50% of the ownership interests, or as otherwise required by law. Upon dissolution, Acme Ventures, LLC's debts and liabilities will be paid or provided for first, with any remaining assets distributed to the members in accordance with their ownership interests, unless this agreement provides otherwise.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Adopted and agreed to by all members:

Member: _______________________ Date: _______________
Member: _______________________ Date: _______________
Member: _______________________ Date: _______________
(Add additional signature lines as needed.)

Upon dissolution, Acme Ventures, LLC's debts and liabilities will be paid or provided for first, with any remaining assets distributed to the members in accordance with their ownership interests, unless this agreement provides otherwise.
